summary: The respondent assessee was assessed to wealth tax for the assessment years 1965 66, 1966 67 and 1967 68. The Wealth Tax Officer included a sum of Rs.3,10,623 as the value of the assets of the assessee on the valuation dates being March 31, 1966 and March 31, 1967. The Wealth tax Officer included a sums of Rs.2,10,063 as the value on the valuation date. The Wealthtax Officer included a further sum of Rs,3,10.623 as its value on the date of valuation. The WealthTax Officer included a portion of the net wealth of the assessee in the assessment years 1966 67 and 1966 68. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner and the Tribunal held that interest was liable to be included in the wealth tax assessments of the assessee. The Tribunal also held that interest could be included in wealth tax assessments. In the reference under section 27(1) (a) of the Wealth Tax Act, the Tribunal held against the assessee. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the assessee that interest was payable on accrual basis (though not realised) on the accountstandings of the money lending business, the accounts of the assessee being maintained on cash basis, not realised on thestandings of money lending business were liable to be excluded in the wealth Tax assessments. Dismissing the reference, ^ HELD: 1. The computation of the net assets of the assesee by the Wealth Tax Officer, the asset would fetch if sold in the open market on the valuation day, though not realised on account of the financial activities of the assessee, bar those expressly excepted by the statute, are to be taken into account, and it is immaterial whether the assessee employs one system of accounting or another. [310B C] 2. The method of accounting, mercantile or cash or hybrid is of no relevance for the purpose of determining the assets of an assessee. The system of accounting, or mercantile, mercantile or hybradrid is of any relevance for the purposes of determining the net wealth. [310C] 3. The method adopted by the assessee in determining the net assets is the relevant period under the Wealth Tax Acts. The method followed by the assessee is not the relevant period. The method is not the same as the valuation date but the valuation date as would have been adopted in respect of the net asset of the assessee at the end of the "previous year" taking into account the financial activities. [310D] 4. The method employed by the assessee for determining the net asset is the relevant date. The method used by the assessee to determine the net assets on the valuationdate is not the basis of the valuation date, but the valuation dates as would have gone into the valuation date in terms of the last day of the "last day of the income tax "previous year". [310E] 5. The method which is adopted by the Wealth tax Officer is not the correct method of accounting. The method for determining the assets is the method of accounting adopted by the assesee. The method to determine the assets of a assessee is the relevant accounting date. The computation is the relevant year under the Wealth tax Act.

The respondent was a civilian employee of the Central Administrative Tribunal. He was dismissed from service on the ground that he had been convicted by a criminal court for an offence punishable under section 302 IPC. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of dismissal. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The High Cou rt held that the respondent was not entitled to the benefit of the provisions of the Act. The High court also held that the order of the Tribunal was not justified. The respondent challenged the order of his dismissal before this Court by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts have no jurisdiction to interfere with the order of punishment. The High Commis sion of the Tribunal is not for the Court to consider whether the ground alone would have weigh ed with the authority in dismissing the public servant. The High Cour t has no jurisdiction to review the penalty imposed on the respondent. [501C D] 2. The High courts have no jurisdiction in interfering with the order imposing a lesser penalty on the respondent because in respect of some of the findings but not even the findings as to substantial misdemeanour for which the punishment can lawfully be imposed, it is not for this Court to consider the question whether the penalty of dismissal from service imposed upon the appel lant was too harsh or excessive. [502D] 3. The High. Court has no jurisdiction in a case of dismissal from servi cial service. The High tution has no jurisdiction, if the findings of the Tribunal are "unreasonable" or "unreasonable". [502E] 4.

The respondent landlord filed a suit for a declaration and injunction to restrain the appellants from dispossessing him from the property known as 'Palmar Oiteral dole Predio Aiva Aoiva Aova Aoiva ' comprising seven lots of coconut grove situated at a Caranzalem belonging to respondent No.1. The Trial Court decreed the suit. The first appellate court dismissed the suit. In second appeal the High Court held that the suit was barred by Order 2 Rule 2(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure. In second second appeal the appellant contended that the suit being barred by Order II Rule 2(2) of the Civil Procedure Code, the jurisdiction of the Civil Court was barred by the principle of res judicata in view of section 7 read with section 58(2) and section 58(3) and that the suit having been dismissed as the Trial Court came to the conclusion that the plaintiff was no more in possession of the property in respect of which he claimed to be a lessee, the suit was not maintainable. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The jurisdiction of the civil court is expressly barred by Order 1 Rule 2(1) of the CPC. [1032D] 2. The jurisdiction is vested in the Mamlatdar under section 7 of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948. The jurisdiction, therefore, vested in the Civil Court is expressly barred from deciding the same in view of Section 7 read with Section 58(2). [1032E] 3. The jurisdiction vested in the civil court stands wholly barred by virtue of section 58(1) and 58(2), specifically bars the jurisdiction of all other courts to settle, decide or deal with any question which is by or under the Act required to be settled, decided and dealt with by any patent authority to settle, deciding or deal with such question which is or by or under any Act required to he settled, decided or dealt with by the Mamlatdar. [1033E F] 4. The jurisdiction conferred on the Mamlatdar under Section 7 readwith Section 58(1)(2) is not vested in the Revenue Court. The jurisdiction to decide or deal is vested in a Civil Court as incidental to the grant of relief claimed in the suit. [1034F] 5. The jurisdiction under Section 7 of the Act is vested in Civil Court as ancillary to the grant or refusal of relief claimed. The jurisdiction extends to the Civil Court and not to the Civil Courts. [1035E] 6. The jurisdiction in the instant case is vested in civil court. The jurisdiction was not vested in Civil Courts. The jurisdiction has been conferred on the Civil Court by Section 58(3). The jurisdiction is, therefore, not vested in a civil court. [1036F] 7. The jurisdiction can be exercised by the Civil Court only if the question is whether a person is a deemed tenant or a deemed tenant was required to be decided by the Mamlatdar and the jurisdiction of Civil Court is specifically barred by sub section (2) of Section 58. [1037F] 8. The jurisdiction cannot be exercised by a Civil Court in a suit instituted in a Civil court. [1138F] 9. The jurisdiction which is vested in an Civil Court is impliedly barred by sub Section (2) and is not vested by the Civil Courts in the Civil Courts, but is vested in it only if the Civil Court has jurisdiction to try the suit. It is not open to the Civil court to give any relief to the landlord by way of possession of the agricultural land. [1039F] 10. The jurisdiction vests in the Civil court is expressly excluded by sub section 2 of Section 58(4) of the Act. [1040F] 11. The jurisdiction lies in the Civil courts.

The petitioners are carpenters in Government service. They are termed as daily rated employees. They claim that the Corporation has reduced its overheads and maintained only the administrative staff in the production centers at different parts of the State and other parts of the country and abroad. The petitioners are carpenterers. They claim to be paid the same wages as carpenters or in the alternative, the minimum wages payable for similar work in the construction industry. The petitioners claim that the pay admissible to them is par with their counterparts in the Government service. The petitioners contended that the Corporation had adopted the minimum wages paid for similar work. The Court, however, directed the Central Government to fix the pay scale of the petitioners on par with their counter parts doing identical work under the same employer. The Court also directed the Central Govern ment to fix the salary of the petitioners in par with their juniors. The Court further directed the Central Gov ernment to fix the scale of the petitioner on par with his counterparts doing identical work. The petitioners filed a writ petition in this Court for enforcement of their fundamental right to have "equal pay for equal work" and for enforcement of the right to "equal pay" of equal work. The main object of the Corporation as seen from the Memorandum of Understanding is to preserve the traditional arts and craftsmen in the State and abroad. It is not possible to provide two different pay scales in the same establishment, the principle of equal pay for equal Work is not one of the fundamental rights expressly guaranteed by our Constitution. The principle of equal work cannot be enforced invariably in every kind of service particularly in the area of professional services. The principle has to be read into Article 14 of the Constitution. The petitioners have been employed by a company incorporated under the . By the general description of their job, one cannot come to the conclusion that every carpenters are equal to the other in the performance of his work. The principle is not oneof the fundamental rights specifically guaranteed by our constitution. The principle cannot be enforced. The Court while rejecting the claim of the petitioners, observed that the principle of "equal pay For equal work" has no mechanical application in every case of similar work. It was also held that the principle has to, be read into article 14 of the Consti tution of India. The principle will have to be read in the light of all the previous decisions of this Court. The principle would be applicable only to skilled and unskilled work. The State cannot deny any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the law or equal protection of law and also to Article 16 which declares that there should be equality of pay for equal works. The principle must depend upon the nature of the work done, it cannot be judged by the mere volume of work, there may be qualitative difference as regards reliability and responsibility. The principle can be invoked invariably in every case where there is a discrimination amongst the same set of employees by the same master in fixing the scales of pay and other conditions of service.

The appellant, who was the sole executor of the will, executed a will in respect of certain properties. The will was written in one room and Lakshmamma was lying in the adjoining room and it was after the will was written that the scribe went into the adjoining room. The testator 's case was that after the death of his father Sadagopalopalachar, her husband Narayana lyengar became the absolute owner of all the properties and so Lakshmamma became the absolute owners of all the property and so Lakshmaamma was not competent in law to make a will in the sense that it represented her intentions. The High Court, however, held that the will was not proved to be the last will and that it was the will in the light of these circumstances that it was her will in the mind that it was she will in the manner of writing the will. The High court, however, found that the will had been written in one space and Lakshmammal had understood its contents and the effect of the dispositions and put her signature to the will. Held, that the will in question was not proved. The High, Court was in error in coming to the conclusion that the will set up by the appellant on the plea that it was not shown that the testatrix fully understood the contents of the will to the testatrix and she understood the nature and effect of its contents. The High. Court was in wrong in coming to that conclusion. The evidence of the appellant was clearly inconsistent with the appellant 's case about previous instructions and so it would be difficult to treat the evidence of this witness as suffi cient to prove that the testatrix was in a sound disposing state of mind and that it had been written by the scribe as he dictated the contents from the draft. The evidence about previous instructions was not corroborated by the appellant. The High , Court was in a wrong position in coming to a conclusion that the testatrix had understood its terms and the effect and the effect thereof. The evidence was clearly inconsistent and inconsistent with the respondent 's case regarding previous instructions and it would be impossible to treat the testimony of this witness in law inasmuch as he thought that the evidence about previous instruction was read out to the testatrix.

The appellant company was engaged in the manufacture of Arcinema Arcinum, and was also engaged in the manufacturing of Arcins. The appellant company was also engaged as a dealer in the manufacture and sale of Arcocons. The appellant was also engaged to manufacture Arcininum, which was used to manufacture Arbocons. It was also engaged for the manufacture of "cinema" and "accessories" and "all parts of motor vehicles". The appellant company, in its turn, manufactured Arcinam, and used to manufacture "cinum" and "cinumatic tyres" falling under entry No. 4 of the 1st Schedule of the Andhra Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1957. The appellant, however, claimed that the goods were "electrical goods" falling under Entry No. 4 and not under Entry No, 4 of the Schedule 1 of the Act. The Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal, the final order of the departmental authority under the Act, allowed the application for adducing expert evidence to determine the question whether the goods were carbons manufactured by the appellant company. The High Court, however, held that the main use of the expression "electrical articles" in Entry No.4 of the 1 st Schedule of the Act, was not "electrical commodities" and that the expression "accessories used in the schedule to describe goods which may have been manufactured for agricultural purposes merely because some of them are also sold to agriculturists for agricultural purposes. The High court, however, allowed the appeal of the appellant company, holding that the main purpose of the entry was to include "electrical products" and that it was not necessary that the goods should be "electrical" in the schedule. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The expression "accessory" in Entry Nos. 4 and 5 of the 1.2 of the Schedule to the Act, is not "electric goods" but includes "accessories". [755G] 2. The expression 'accessories" in Entry 4 of the schedule refers to goods which may be manufactured for use as an aid or addition. It is not necessary that a purchaser makes some use of it. The word "accessories", in Entry No., 4, refers to goods manufactured for use for a particular kind of instrument of gadget. The word 'accessories ' is used in Entry No,4, in the schedule, in which it occurs. The entry refers to goods of which description in a schedule to describe them, would not cease to be covered by an entry merely because some purchaser makes some other use of it, and the entry refers to "accessories." [755H; 755A] 3. The expression `accessories" is used in the entry itself considered in the context in which it occur. The entry itself considered the use which is generally made of the articles of gadtget, only where an entry relates to parts manufactured for use in projectors or other cinematographic equipment. The entry, therefore, could only be satisfactorily determined in the light of the language of the entry itself. [755B C] 4. The expression, "accessories " in the schedule refers only to goods which are used for the purpose of equipment or accessories connected with the main purpose. The word `accessories ' in Entry No.. 4, in the Schedule refers to goods used for the purposes of equipment or accessory. The word, "accessory", in Entry Nos., 4 and 5, refers to "all parts" as well as "accessories thereof". [756F G] 5. The expression is used in a sense of a word, and it is not necessary to define the expression "all parts". [757F] 6. The expression used in the Schedule is "electrical". The word "electrical", in Entry 4, refers only to "electrical items".

The appellant was the trustee of a temple of the Kumaran Koil. The trusteeship of the temple was "hereditary" and the appellant was the hereditary trustee. The respondents took a different view and proceeded on the basis that the trusteeship of a Kumaran Koils was hereditary. The Subordinate Judge held that the appellant was a hereditary trustee within the meaning of section 6(9) of the Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1959. The Subordinate judge held that the trustees of the temple were hereditary. The respondents appealed to the High Court. The High Court held that the appointment of the appellant was hereditary and the suit was not barred by limitation. The respondents came to this Court by special leave. The question for consideration was whether the appellant was an hereditary trustee within section 6(1) of the Act. HELD: (1) The definition of hereditary trustee in section 6(4) of the Hindu Religious Endowments act, 1959 is identical in both the Acts. The definition of the trustee is identical in the sense that on the death of an existing mahant, his chela does not succeed to the office as a matter of course, because the successor owes his title to the deceased under the law, the office must be transmitted to the successor according to some definite rules of descent by which the successor accordingto some definite rules or usage of the particular institution except where the rule of succession is laid down by the founder himself who created the endowment. [446 B C] (2) The artificial definition of hereditary trustees in section 6 (9) of Act 19 of 1951 must be construed along with the phrase "succession to this office" and when so construed that part of the definition would only apply where the ordinary rules of succession under the Hindu law are modified by usage and succession has to be determined in accordance with the modified rules. [447 C] (3) The artificial definitions of hereditary trustees are in the nature of property. The definition is not exhaustive and it is not possible to say that there is a succession of hereditary trustee. [448 D] (4) The artificial meaning of hereditary trustee is in the nature Of property. The word "successor" is not defined in the Act. The word 'succession ' is not defined. The word is not defined by the Act. It is not defined either in the Act or in the Act, but in the context of the Act, it is not necessary to say that the definition of hereditary hereditary trustee in the Act is identical in its sense. [449 E] (5) The artificial term "successed" in section 6 of the Act must be construed together with the phrase 'successor '. The definition would only be applicable where the ordinary rule of succession under Hindu law is modified by usage.

The appellant was charged with murder under section 302 IPC and sentenced to death. The prosecution alleged that the deceased was last seen with the appellant on the date of occurrence and that he was sleeping on a bench outside his cattle shed in the open space. The prosecution case was that the deceased chased the accused and was sleeping on the southern side of the sluice of the north Boothagudi channel. The prosecution also alleged that the appellant was sleeping on his eastern parapet of the sjuice of the south Boothagududi channel. On the other hand, the prosecution alleged that PW 4 was a leperate and was sleeping in a bench outside the cattle shed in front of his cattle shed. The prosecution further alleged that the accused was sleeping on one side of the Sluice of north Bootagudi channel. PW 4 was also sleeping on the eastern parapet. The prosecution, therefore, alleged that the first information report was lodged by PW 4 at about 10.00 P.M. on April 26, 1971 at about 10 P.M., and that the first informant was sleeping on an average of about 10 Pm. on the southern part of the sauice of the east Boothagu channel. The trial court acquitted the second accused, who was convicted under section 302/34 IPC. The High Court, however, acquitted the second appellant, holding that the prosecution had failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court had not considered the intrinsic quality of the evidence of PW 4 and that the High court had not considered its intrinsic quality of evidence of PW4. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High court was not right in assessing the quality of the testimony of PW 4. The High. Court was not even right that PW 4 stood wholly corroborated by the contents of the FIR. The High, Court was not right that PW4 stood wholly corroborated from the contents of exhibit P1 FIR. [707C] 2. The High Courts were not right in holding that the evidence of PWs 1, 2 and 3 was corroborated by the version given out by PW 4. [708D] 3. The High Curt was not right, even if it was not possible to adopt that course in this case.

The respondents were the heirs and legal representatives of Amarchand who died in the previous year. The respondents were the legal representatives of the deceased Amarchand. The respondents claimed that the income received by them before his death should be deemed by the fiction incorporated in sub section (1) to be income received by Amarchand and liable to tax under section 24B of the Income tax Act. The Income tax Officer found that the respondents were the owners and legal representatives and that the income was liable to tax. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner, however, held that the income of the deceased was liable to be assessed to income tax under section 23B of the Act. The Appellate Tribunal held that the Income tax Officer was entitled to assess the total income of the respondents under section 24 B of the Act and that the Income Tax Officer was entitled only to assess the income received after his death. The High Court, on a reference, held that on a correct interpretation of section 24B the amounts which were received by the heirs and representatives of Amar Chand were liable to tax as income received by the deceased person and those were not liable to be taxed in the several years of assessment. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The fiction is limited to the cases provided in the three sub sections of section 24 B and cannot be extended beyond the object for which it was enacted. The fiction is confined to the cases providing in the three subsections of section 24A and cannot be extend beyond the object of which it was made. [707 D] (ii) The fiction of law is limited to cases provided in section 24B and cannot be extension beyond the object provided in the third sub sections of s.24B. [708 D] (iii) The fiction cannot be extended within the object for Which it was enacted and cannot be limited to the case provided in the 3 sub sections of the section. [709 E] (iv) The fiction, by fiction of law, became assessees as provided in that section but in that fiction the legal representatives have been treated as assessees for the purpose of assessment in the several assessment years. [710 E] (v) The fiction does not extend beyond the objects for which it is enacted. The legal representatives have not been treated as the assessees for the purposes of assessment in any of the three sub clauses of section 24. [711 E] (vi) The fiction extends to the cases of the three subsections only. The fiction does no extend beyond the purpose for which it has been enacted. [712 E] (vii) The fiction applies to cases provided by the three sub section of section 24 and cannot be confined beyond the object mentioned in the three subsection of section 24(1). [712 F] (viii) The fiction has not been extended beyond the objects of the three subsection.

The petitioners who were members of the Andhra Pradesh State Public Employment (Requirement to Residence) Rules, 1959, challenged the validity of the said Rules on the ground that they were violative of articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. The petitioners contended that the impugned Rules were violative of article 14 of the Constitution and that the impugned rules were violative of Articles 14 and 16. The petitioners also contended that the Rules were ultra vires the Constitution. Held, that the power given to Parliament under article 35(a) of the Constitution to make any law providing for residence in a part of a State was not unguided and uncanalised. The power to make a declaration and leaving the details to be filled in by the rule making power of the Central or State Governments to provide residence in a particular part of the State was not arbitrary or uncanalised. It was not open to the State Government to make a law in respect of a part of the state. The power was given to Parliament and could make any law on the subject as the article was construed as conferring a power to make any provision for residence in the State or Union territory prior to the appointment or employment. The power of the State Government under article 35 (a) was not unguided or uncanalised and it was not open for the State Government or the Union territory to make any such law. The power given to the Central or the State Governments to make any legislation in regard to a class or classes of employment or appointment to an office under the State was valid. The power conferred on Parliament under article 32 was not unguided, uncanalised and uncanalised and was not arbitrary. The power could not be exercised arbitrarily or capriciously. The power under article 32 could be exercised only in the case of a law prescribing a requirement of residence in a State or Union Territory. The power is given to Parliament to make any laws providing for residence within that State or Union territories prior to the appointed or employment. It is not open to Parliament to prescribe any requirement as to residence in a specified part of the Union or State or to any requirement as residence in a specific part of the States. The power can be exercised only when it is exercised in a manner which is not arbitrary or capricious. The power may be exercised in a proper manner and in a proper case, not arbitrarily or capricically. The power must be exercised in the proper manner and not arbitrarily or whimsically. The exercise of the power must be in a proper and reasonable manner and not arbitrary. It must be exercised bona fide and in a just manner. The power cannot be exercised arbitrarily and whimsically. It must not be exercised in arbitrary or capricious manner. The exercise must be in accordance with the law made by Parliament. The power has to be exercised in accordance with law made by the Parliament. The exercise is not arbitrary, capricious or whimsical. The power, therefore, must be exercised within the limits prescribed by the law made in the interest of the general public. The power should be exercised in good faith and in a fair and just manner. It must also be exercised in conformity with the principles of natural justice. The power exercised must be in conformity with law made in that behalf. The power which is exercised must be exercised reasonably and in a reasonable manner. The principles of natural Justice must be observed to be the principles of fair play and natural justice. It must, therefore, be held that the power conferred on the Parliament under article 368 is not arbitrary and capricious. The exercise, therefore, is not arbitrary.

The appellant was a postman attached to the Bulandshahr post office. He was tried for offences under sections 467 and 471 of the Indian Penal Code and in two of them, for offences under section 52 of the Indian Post Office Act, 1898 (VI of 1898) and in two, them for offences under Sections 467 and 471, of the Indian penal Code. The trial court acquitted the appellant but the High Court acquitted him. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The High Court was in error in holding that though the prosecution had merely shown that the registered letters were recovered from an almirah in the house in which the appellant lives jointly with his father and of which the key was furnished by the father, the almirah contained a large number of articles belonging to the father and since the key was produced by the appellant 's father, the appellant could not be said to have secreted them from the mere fact that they were found in the almirah which was said to have been in his exclusive possession. The appellant company was a company carrying on the business of manufacturing and selling cotton yarn. It was carrying on the same business as a manufacturer of yarn. It had its registered office at Hyderabad. It had a branch office at Hyderabad and its directors were also carrying on the said business. The appellant company was carrying on its business in the manufacture and sale of yarn. The appellant was a company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1913. It was registered under the Companies act, 1956. The appellant, a company, was carrying on business in the production and sale of cotton yarn. The company was carrying out its business in its own name. The appellant 's company was carrying its business in yarn. The respondent company was carrying the business of selling cotton yarn and selling cotton. The appellant filed a complaint against the 1st respondent company and its directors for failure to Me with the Registrar of Companies on or before 30 10 1967 the balance sheet and profit and loss account of the company as required under section 220(1) of the Companies Act. The 1st respondent filed a complaint before the Judicial Magistrate, First Class, Hyderabad, under section 134(1)(c) of the , alleging that the 1st appellant company had failed to call a general body meeting and to lay the balance sheet, profit and loss accounts before it could not be laid before a general body. The Magistrate dismissed the complaint. The High Court held that the 1 st appellant company was not liable to be prosecuted under section 134 of the 1913 Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The High Court was in error in holding that the 1.1.1. was not liable under the provisions of the 1913 and the company was not entitled to be prosecuted. [401 D] (2) The High Courts were in error in taking the view that the decision necessarily led to the conclusion that even in a prosecution under section 134, there can be no question of that balance sheet not being adopted or complying with the requirements of section 220(2) of the 1956 Act or section 220 of the 1956. [402 D] (3) The punishment under section 134 is for default in filing copies of the balance sheet or profit and loss Account before it can expose the person responsible to punishment under other provisions of the Act. The punishment under the section is for default. [403 E] (4) The punishment of default under section 134 does not make him liable u/s 134 of the 1956 Acts. The punishment is for default and the person responsible for punishment under other sections of the Act is for default, and the person liable to punishment under the other provisions of that Act is also liable for punishment under the Act. [404 F] (5) The punishment is not for default in making the copies of the Balance sheet or profit & loss account which are laid before a special general body meeting before an annual general meeting. The punishment of the default is for default only. [405 F] (6) The punishment in section 134 is not for failure to call a meeting as a defence to the charge under his sections. The punishment in Section 134 is for failure to file the balance sheet. The punishment cannot be laid before the general body meeting. [407 F] (7) The punishment for default is for failure of the company to file the list of the prescribed general body meeting, and for failure to do so is made punishable under sub section (4) of section 134 of that Act. [414 F] (8) The punishment imposed under section 134 cannot be said to be for default in the filing of copies of the balances sheet or profit loss account. [408 G] (9) The punishment cannot therefore be said to have been imposed for default in not filing copies of balance sheet or the profit loss account before it can be said to amount to a breach of the provisions of section 134.

The appellant was convicted under section 5(1) of the West Bengal Special Courts Act, 1947, and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for one year. The appellant contended that the provisions of the Act were discriminatory and violative of article 14 of the Constitution and that the provisions for the speedier trial of certain offences were discriminatory and that the provision for the speer trial of offences or classes of cases should be tried by a special court according to the special procedure prescribed by the Code of Criminal Procedure. Held, that the object of the Act was to provide for the spelledier trial and the object being, as expressed in its preamble, that the preamble was to be read as a part of section 5(I) of the Act, and that the object being that the preamble should be read as part of section5(1) and the proper interpretation to be put upon the sub section would be to suggest that the object by itself cannot be the basis of the classification of offences or the cases, for, in the absence of any special circumstances which may dis pinguish one offence or class of offences or class of cases from another offence or class or classes of offences, or classes of offence, or classes or cases from another offences, or class of offence, and if any charge of discrimination can be levelled at all, it can be levelled only against the act of the executive authority if the Act is misused. The object of the legislation is to provide for speedier trials of certain offences and classes of cases, and if the Act itself is misused, it can only be made against the act or the cases which in the opinion of the State Government would require speedier Trial. The object is to provide speediertrial of certain offences, and in the opinion Of the legislature certain offences may require more expeditious trial than other offences and this was a good enough classification. The object being, the preamble is to be read in the context of the Act as expressed in the preamble. The object was to provide spelledi trial of certain offence and classes of offences or of classes of cases. The object, therefore, was to provide speedy trial of certain cases, and to provide speedy justice to the accused. The object in the present case was to provide expeditious trial of certain other offences and classes or cases, and that in the opinion, the Special Court had no jurisdiction to try those cases. The provisions for the speedy trial of offences and classes Of cases, or classes Of cases were not, therefore, discriminatory in so far as it authorised the State Government to direct the offences, which in its judgment, required speedier trail of certain offences. The object which was to provide a speedy trial of such offences was, therefore, the object of that Act as expressed by the preamble.

The appellant was appointed as a Professor of Radiology in the respondent Institute of Medical Sciences, New Delhi. He was promoted as a Professor in the said Institute on the recommendation of a Departmental Promotion Committee. The appellant was appointed to the post of Professor of Radiotherapy in the Maulana Azad Medical College, New Delhi, and was confirmed in the said post. The appellant challenged the order of confirmation of his services by a writ petition before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellant contended that the designation of the appellant as a Radiologist in the Ma XLI Azad Medical College was akin to that of an Associate Professor of Radiologist (ex officio) and that the appellant possessed the qualification and experience prescribed in the Central Health Service (Amendment) Rules, 1966. The High court dismissed the writ appeal. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the designation as a Radiographer was a teaching post and the appellant having been substantively appointed to the said post of Associate Professor of the concerned speciality as required under the Central Health Services (Amendment) Act, 1966, the post of Associate Professors of Radiology (ex officio), was a teaching hospital attached to the Maulana Nehru Medical College, Delhi, and the appellant who had been substantively appointed as a Radiologists in the Ma Lady Azad Medical College had actually teaching the students of the Maulana Gandhi Azad Medical College. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The Ministry of Health cannot be heard to say that the appellant has not acquired the status of an Associate professor of Radiology with effect from October 9, 1964, particularly when the Central Government have been utilizing his services as such for teaching the post graduate and under graduate students of theMaulana Azad Medical college. [812C D] 2. The Ministry cannot be heard tO say that the Appellant has not acquired a status of an Assistant Professor of Radiological (ex officio). [813E] 3. The Ministry is not a party to the appeal. The Ministry has been utilizing the services of such Assistant Professors of Radiological and the appellant has been utilized his services as an Associate Professor in the Maheed Azad Medical College for the M.D., M.D.S., M.B.B.S. courses of studies for the last 17 years. [814C D] 4. The Ministry, of Health cannot, however, be heard to state that the appellant had not acquired the requisite experience and requisite experience for appointment to the post. [815E] 5. The Ministry does not give him a right to hold the post of Assistant Professor of the relevant speciality as required by the Central Health service (Amendment) rules, 1966. [816F] 6. The Ministry may not be heard to have the appellant retired from service on the ground that he had not acquired any status of an Additional Professor of Radiography. [817F] 7. The Ministry should be heard to determine the question of his eligibility for such promotion or appointment. [818F] 8. The Ministry shall be heard to decide the question of eligibility for such appointment or appointment. The Ministry will be heard to hear the appellant and the respondent.

The workmen of the appellant company were employed by the respondent company as casual workers in the appellant company. The workmen were paid wages at the rate of three months ' basic wages and dearness allowance. The workmen claimed that they were entitled to the minimum wages at the average level of 'wages in the Company on the basis of the minimum wage prevailing in the other comparable industries in the region. The Tribunal held that the minimum wage in the Company was to be fixed at the average levels of 'wages ' in the other industrial concerns in the region which could be compared with the Company. The Tribunal also accepted the contention of the workmen that the minimum wages in the Company were higher than the minimum wages paid by the Company, but failed to fix the minimum wages. The Tribunal, however, held that the Tribunal was justified in fixing the minimum wages on the basis that the minimum Wages in the Company should be fixed at Rs. 95. The Tribunal further held that the workmen were entitled to higher wages on the principle of 'equal pay for equal work '. The Tribunal accordingly held that the ' Minimum Wages ' in the Company 's case was not rigid and, it was not necessary that the minimum ' wages in the company should be fixed on the basis 'of the minimum wage prevalent in the other industries in that region. The appellant company appealed to this Court. HELD : The Tribunal was expected to decide the dispute only as referred to it and at the time of reference, at the time the Award was given, the accounts for the year 1962 63 were available. The Tribunal was therefore expected to decide this dispute only as refer to it and not as to the Tribunal. [712 B] The Tribunal was required to decide the question as to whether the minimum wage was a consolidated wage consisting of the two 678 elements of basic wage and dearness allowance, and the dearness allowance was ignored. [713 C] The Tribunal, in its award, held that, if the minimum wage at the average rate of three month ' basic wages was separately payable, the bonus was calculated on the basis Of the minimum wage existing in the Company and the Company had agreed to exclude these classes of workers in regard to payment of bonus. The Tribunal therefore, held that there was no justification for departing from the figure of Rs.95 which was the average minimum wage payable by those industries in the other two 678 elements. [714 D E] The Tribunal had rightly held that the total minimum wage in respect of the appellant was Rs.95. The Tribunal had also accepted the same as being comparable industries in that area. The Tribunal 's award, therefore, was not justified in interfering with the Tribunal 's decision on the ground that under the Agreement of 1959, the workmen and the Company were also entitled to the same costs of this appeal.

The appellant, who was at the commencement of the Indian Income tax (Amendment) Act, 1939, carried on business in the old firm, which was carrying on business in that firm, for the document of October 30, 1943, which was a deed of October 30. 1943, was registered in the name of the appellant. The appellant claimed that the business must have been charged to tax under the Indian Income Tax Act, 1918, and that the business should have been charged under the Indian Incometax Act, 1918. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner, however, held that the business of the appellant was liable to tax under section 25(4) of the Income tax Act, 1918 and that the appellant was not liable to pay tax for the period between April 13, 1938 and March 28, 1939. The Appellate Tribunal, however, allowed the appeal and held that the appellant had not been able to prove that the business was carried on by him in 1948, and that, therefore, the business must be deemed to have been carried on in 1948. The appellant appealed to the Appellate Tribunal. The Tribunal held that the assessee was entitled to the benefits of section 25(3) of the Act, and that as a result of this splitting up there was a discontinuance of the original business at the date of the partition and on such discontinuance, the family became entitled to relief under section 25 (4) of that Act. The Tribunal, however held that the partnership business must have actually been charged to income tax under the Act of 1918 and that, in the absence of a succession by another person, the business could not be said to have been validly carried on in the original business. The Tribunal also held that the firm was entitled to relief. The High Court, however, dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The Tribunal was right in holding that the business carried on by the two independent firms, for the documents of October 30 and March 28 1939, was liable to be taxed under the Act. [107 C] (ii) The Tribunal had rightly held that the two sub sections were not applicable to the case. The Tribunal was wrong in holding that there was a continuity of the original firm and that the assessee had not been taken on the original business even though the partnership business was carried out in 1948. [107 D] (iii) The Tribunal erred in holding that in sub section (3) of section 25 of the Act the business must continue to be carried on in that firm. [107 E] (iv) The Tribunal, therefore, was wrong in not holding that the assessee could not be treated as a Hindu undivided family. [107 F] (v) The Tribunal rightly held that there was no succession by another. The Tribunal erred, in holding that it was not necessary to prove that there was succession by another, and that there was, therefore, a succession by the other. [107 G] (vi) The Tribunal wrongly held that the income, profits and gains of the said period were assessable under the Act, 1918 as income, profits or gains of the previous year. [107 A] (vii) The Tribunal correctly held that the original business of the assessee was liable to income tax for the years 1948 49 and 1949 50. [107 B] (viii) The Tribunal also erred in holding, that the business in respect of which alone the benefit of section 25 (3) was on succession to a person who, on April 1, 1939, was carrying on any business on which tax was at any time charged under the Act for the period from April 13, 1939, to March 28, 1940, was succeeded in such capacity by another person.

The appellant, a Hindu widow, filed a suit for partition of the properties of the joint family. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court dismissed the appellant 's appeal. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the suit properties belonged to the joint family and that the suit property belonged to the Joint family and that there was no prior partition and that the plaintiff was entitled to a 7/24th share in the joint family properties. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The interest of a Hindu Mist coparcener shall be deemed to be the share in the property that would have been allotted to him if a partition of the property had taken place immediately before his death. The fictional, therefore, expedient to the simple expedient, that the interest of a Mitakshara coparcener shall be presumed to be the shares in the property which the deceased had at the time of his death. [724B C] (2) The proviso to section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, is essentially a fictional, that the interests of a Hindu Mitakshara coparcener shall, be deemed to have been allotted, if a partition had taken place in the coparcenary property, since there is none in the instant case, by the application of the rules of intestate succession contained in sections 8, 9 and 10 of the Hindu Law. [725F G] (3) The fictional fiction, that the share of a Hindu coparcener shall be determined according to the terms of the testamentary instrument, if any, made by the deceased, irrespective of whether he was entitled to claim partition or not. [726G] (4) The fictionally expedient to the actual partition of the coparcenary property is to find out the share which the deceased has in the coparcenary properties. The fictionally, that the estate of a Hindu coparcenary property would devolve by survivorship upon the surviving members of the coparcenary and not in accordance with the provisions of the Act. [727A] (5) The fiction is that the interest which a Hindu Mitakshara coparcenary property would have been given to him if the partition of the family property had taken places immediately before his lifetime. The fiction is, therefore, imperative in the very nature of things, and as the very first step, to ascertain the share of the deceased in the coparcenary, the plaintiff 's share must be ascertained by adding the share to which she is entitled at a notional partition of the joint property. [728C D] (6) The fiction, however, is not to be readily inferred. The fiction, therefore, is not readily inferred. [729D] (7) The fiction created by the proviso is not to operate as a fiction. The fiction created is not to have the effect of a fiction. [730E] (731C] (8) The fiction operates only when the property is allotted to a coparcener. The fiction operates in the absence of a fiction, and the fiction is not to apply to a case where the property is not allotted to a person. [732D] (9) The fiction does not operate as a mere fiction. The Explanation is not to affect the fiction. The effect of the fiction is that if a partition takes place immediately before the death of a coparcener it is necessary in the very fact of things, that the heir will get his share in the coparcenary. [733E] (10) The fiction has to be gathered from the language of the proviso. The fiction has been introduced by the Explanation. 1 to section 6. [734F] (11) The fiction cannot be extended to cases where the property has been allotted to a member of the coparcenary. The fiction does operate only when the coparcenary property has been partitioned. [735F] (12) The fiction must be lifted from the language used in the Explanation. The fiction must, therefore, be lifted from a reading of the Explanation.

The appellant Corporation was established in the year 1962. The appellant Corporation was a public sector undertaking. The appellant was appointed as a Class III employee in the Corporation on or after 1st September, 1956. The age of retirement of the employees of the Corporation was 60 years. The appellant 's services were terminated by the Corporation on the ground that the age of retirement was 60 years and the employees of Class I and Class II appointed to the service of the Corporation on 1st September 1956 were not entitled to continue in service beyond the age of 58 years. The Corporation terminated the services of the employees on the ground of their being promoted to Class III and Class IV posts. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the termination of the services of its employees. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant Corporation that the employees of a public sector Undertaking were not entitled for the benefit of the age of superannuation of the employees who had entered service of the appellant corporation on or after the 1st September 1961 and that the employees belonging to Class I and II appointed to Class I or Class II appointed on or after January 1, 1956 were not eligible to continue in the service of that Corporation on or before 1st September 1960. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The employees of the appellantCorporation after 1st October, 1956 were entitled to continue beyond the age Of 58 years only because they had been promoted to Class I post after 1st November, 1956. [223B] 1.2 The employees of a Public Sector Undertaking who had entered the service of a Corporation after 1st January, 1956 were also not entitled to continued in service beyond that date. [223C] 1.3 The employees of an Undertaking who had joined the service of an Undertaking after 1st Sept., 1956 were not governed by the settlement and the amendment of the regula tion 19 in the year 1977, and the amendment was made in the year 1978. [223D] 1.4 The employees of public sector undertakings who had entered into service of the Undertaking after 1 st September, 1956 were governed by the Settlement and the amendment made by the new sub regulation (2) of regulation 19 empowered the appointing authority to extend at its discretion the service of any employee of the Corporation after giving him three months ' notice or salary in lieu thereof. The amendment made by sub regulation (1) of regulation 20 empowered the appointing authori ty to extend at his discretion the service any employee of a public Sector Undertaking who was employed after 1st of September, 1956, to retire on completion of 58 years of age subject to the usual clause relating to premature retirement. The amendment was made by sub clause (2) to sub regulation (3) of regulation 18 empowered the appointing authorities to extend at their discretion the service or class II service of any employees of the Undertaking who had been employed after 1 st of September,1956. [223E F] 1.5 The amendment made in the regulation 19(2) of the Staff Regulations, 1960 was not in terms applicable to the employees who were appointed directly to any post belonging to Class II or Class III. The amendment of the Regulation 19(2), 1960 was not applicable to the employee who had entered services of the Corporation before 1st of October, 1956. It was only in 1965 under the settlement and amendment of the Regulations, 1960 as amended in the year1977, and the amended Regulation 19(1) of the Regulations was not applicable.

The letter referred to the letter of appellant and said "on a perusal of the contents thereof a prima facie case is made out. The deponent tenders his apology to this Hon 'ble Court for the same and prays for its acceptance. [246G] 3. The deponent tendered his apology to the Court. The deponent did not do anything. [246A] 4. The deponent has tendered his apology and prayed for its acceptance, and prayed for acceptance of the apology. The contemnor tendered his apology in the Court. [246C] 5. The deponent does not say anything about the contents of the letter and does not say that the contents thereof were incorrect. The deponent states that the contents of that letter were not in accordance therewith. The deponent says that the contents therein were incorrect. [246D] 6. The appellant was a member of the Scheduled Caste of the West Bengal Legislative Assembly from the Khargram Murshidgram Murshidpore. He was a member belonging to a smaller group of Sunri caste. The Tribunal accordingly set aside the election of appellant to be set aside on the ground, that the Saha had formed for the long past. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The appellant belonged to the smaller group of Sahaas. The fact that the Saha was a smaller caste was not a ground to hold that the Sahaas formed a sub caste within the Sunr caste. [389 B C] (ii) The fact that Sahas had originally belonged to a different group of Sahasa, was not a sufficient ground to hold the appellant to be a Sunri. The appellant, a resident of the erstwhile State of Cochin, was assessed to income tax under the Indian Income tax Act, Travancore Cochin, on the ground that the business losses incurred in the erstwhile State were not income from business profits made in the erstwhile state of Cochin. The Income tax Officer assessed the appellant to income tax on the ground, inter alia, that the business loss incurred in the former State of Cochin could not be set off against the business profits made by it in the erstwhile territory of Travancore. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner, on appeal, held that the business profits of the erstwhile state were not income of the appellant and that the business income was not liable to tax under the Income tax Act. The Appellate Tribunal, however, held that business losses incurred by the appellant in the former state of Cochin were not income in any place which was not an Indian State. The High Court, however, took the view that the business expenditure incurred in the latter State of Cochin was not income in the former territory of Travancore and that the losses incurred in that State were not taxable in the former Indian State. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The mere use of the words " income or gains accruing or arising to him within or in an Indian State" in the proviso to sub section (1) of section 24(1) of the Travancore Act, as amended by the Travancore Act (XXIII of 1941), by which another clause (c) was added to section 14(2)(c) of the Indian Act, was to set off against profits and gains accruing or arise within British India or in an existing Indian State. [261 F G] (ii) The mere fact that the word " income" is not used does not justify the construction. The mere use by the words "income or gains accruing" does not justify such construction. [261 G] (iii) The mere user of the words 'income or gains ' in any other head, specially keeping in view the object of the main section i.e. section 24(I) which was to set the off of profits and gains to be set off, against profits and losses arising under the head business in the two territories, i.e., British India and the Indian States, would not be sufficient to restrict the scope of the proviso to the profits and losses incurred in those two territories, namely, British India and Travancore State. [262 A B] (iv) The mere usage of the words in the proviso does not justify an interpretation in favour of the disintegration of the head " business in British India. [262 B] (v) The mere addition of the words to the proviso to section 24(i) which was not to set off the loss of profits or gains under one head, specially kept in view the objects of the main Section i.e section 24(2)(b) of the Act not only affected the generality of the main enactment but also affected the generality Of the main section. [262 C D] (vi) The mere omission of the words used does not support an interpretation in the favour of the appellant.

The respondent was a commissioned officer in the Army. He was dismissed from service by a General Court Martial. He challenged the order of dismissal by a petition under article 226 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that r. 14 of the Army Rules, 1954, including r. 14, of the Army, Rules, 1954 was ultra vires the . The respondent contended that r 14 of the Rules, 1954 had no authority to remove him from service. HELD: The two sections 19 and 45 of the Army Act, 1954, are mutually exclusive. The two sections are, therefore, mutually exclusive. [451 C] The two sections were mutually exclusive. They are mutually exclusive and the Central Government has no power to remove a person from the service. The two provisions are mutually exclusive, and the Central Govern ment has no power under the Act to remove a man from the service, and the order of removal from service under section 19 of the read with r. 14 is therefore ultra vires the Act. [451 D] The two provisions, namely, r. 14 and r. 14 are, therefore mutually exclusive. There may be a valid rule providing for the removal from service. The Central Government has thus no power to removed a person from service. [451 E] The two Sections 19 and 45 are mutually exclusive in nature and the Central Govt. has no power either to remove a member from the service or to suffer such less punishment as is in this Act mentioned.

The conciliation authorities were bound to make their report within 14days but that did no end when the reports were received by the Conciliation officer. The conciliation and if for any reason the Conciliation officer did not make their report, the proceeding could not be held to have concluded.

The Custodian can cancel a lease only if the Custodian has the authority to issue a notice in the prescribed manner. The Custodian cannot cancel a lease without reference to the provisions that it could be exercised notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force. The Custodian, therefore, has the power under section 12 to cancel a licence granted by himself. The Custodian could cancel a lease if the Custodian had the authority to do so. The Custodian was not the authority to pass a fresh order under section 12, and the question of the rights of the appellants in the present appeal was not raised in the petition. The Custodian did not issue any directions with reference thereto. The Custodian therefore could cancel a licence only if the evacuee had the power under that section to cancel the lease. The Custodian 's power under section 10 of the Act was not exhausted. The Custodian in the present proceedings was not the appropriate authority to issue any directions. The Custodian under section 10 could cancel a contract if the Custodian was satisfied that the property was not evacuee property.

The appellant, a newspaper, was engaged in the business of printing and publishing newspapers and other periodical work. The appellant, a news Reporter, was appointed by the Central Government to carry out the provisions of the Working Journalists (Conditions of Service) and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1955. The appellant was appointed as a news Reporter. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the Act and the Rules made thereunder. The High Court accepted the plea of the Ist respondent and declared that the law reports were not newspapers within the meaning of the Act. The High court accepted the plea and declared that there was no newspaper in the State of Orissa and declared that it was not a newspaper. The High, however, held that the law Reports were not newspapers. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Ist Respondent that the law report published by the Ist respondent contains information about the recent events which have taken place in the Supreme Court or in the High Courts which are public bodies and these matters in which the public is interested. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The Act in question is a beneficent legislation which is enacted for the purpose of improving the conditions of service of the employees of the newspaper establishments and hence even if it is possible to have two opinions on the construction of the provisions of that Act, the latest judgment itself is sufficient to make a law report to make it a newspaper. [782C D] 2. The Act is a beneficient legislation which is enacting for the purpose to improve the conditions of the service of the newspaper employees and hence even though the publication of these items may not occupy a substantial part of a law report, the publication of the said articles by itself may not occupy any substantial part of the law report. [785F] 3. The Act does not carry any news and that the public is not interested in them. The Act has been enacted for the purposes of improving the condition of service of employees of newspaper establishments and that it is not essential for a newspaper to conform strictly to the usual pattern of a daily or weekly newspaper or monthly newspaper or a magazine containing news. [786G H] 4. The Act was a beneficent statute which was enacted for the object of improving the working of the employees and of the newspaper establishment. The Act, therefore, is a beneficitable legislation which is designed for the purpose for improving the conditions and service of the employee of the newspaper. [886F] 5. The Act provides for the establishment of a newspaper and the establishment of the newspaper and the establishments of the newspaper, and the establishment and the establishment. The object of the Act is to provide for the establishment and establishment of the newspapers and for the establishment, maintenance and management of the newspaper industry. The Act also provides for the regulation of the working of newspaper establishments. The Act makes it a social welfare legislation which is intended to provide for better protection of the employees. The Act contains a comprehensive legislation for the purpose and implementation of the provisions relating to the establishment and maintenance of newspaper establishments, and the management of the affairs of the newspaper is vested in the State Government.

The appellant was a tenant of the respondent. The respondent was a tenant under the respondent. He was inducted into the premises on 1st of September, 1965. The respondent filed a suit for eviction of the appellant on the ground that he was a tenant and not a sub tenant. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court, however, allowed the revision holding that the respondent was a licensee and not a tenant. The High court, however, held that the respondent had failed to prove that he was in occupation of the premises on the 1st of February, 1973 under a subsisting agreement for leave and licence of the licensor for a period of five years from 1st of October, 1965 till 31st of August, 1970 and it was further held that the appellant was a direct tenant of the premises. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the respondent having been a tenant, the agreement for leave, licence and licence was not put an end to by the appellant and that in any event by filing the application for eviction the appellant licensor had granted an implied licence to the respondent licensee to continue in possession till a decree of eviction was passed in his favour. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The agreement would be construed as a mere licence but as a lease. The agreement was not construed as a merely licence but as an interest in the property, the agreement would be interpreted as a mere licensee. [701C] 2. The agreement is not a lease and as a mere license but as a licence, it is coupled with an interest in property. The agreement does not amount to a licence. The agreement cannot be construed as merely a licence but as licence. [702D] 3. The agreement in question was coupled with an Interest in the property. The contract was coupled with a licence. It was coupled with the interest in the premises. The agreement did not amount to licence. The respondent had been inducted into the property on 1st February, 1973. The agreement could not be construed as an agreement for leave or licence. [0702E] 4. The agreement clearly shows that after 31st March, 1966 the respondent was in occupation and possession of the premises for the period of five year. The agreement therefore was not a lease. [703G] 5. The agreement for leave was coupled with interest in the land, the agreement was coupled with An interest in the building. The agreement also shows that the respondent would be entitled to occupy the premises on a monthly rent of Rs. 500 per month. [704B] 6. The agreement, therefore, clearly shows that the appellant had been inducted as a monthly tenant of the suit premises on 1.2.1973 under a subsisting licence. The tenancy agreement was not a licence but a lease. It was a licence and not a lease, and the appellant was not a licensee. [0704C] 7. The agreement itself shows that after the 31st March 1966 the respondent had granted an express licence to the appellant licensor to continue in occupation till a decree for eviction was passed, he passed an order of eviction against the appellant. The High Courts, therefore, exceeded its jurisdiction under Article 227 of the Constitution.

The appellant company was a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, and was registered under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932. The appellant company was incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956, and was a public limited company. The appellant was a private limited company. It was registered under section 3 of the Indian Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1970. The appellant filed a suit for a declaration that the order of the High Court was illegal and void and that the suit was not maintainable. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court held that the order was final and the appellant was not entitled to the certificate. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The expression "final order" in section 205 of the Government of India Act, 1935, means an order which finally determines the points in dispute and brings the case to an end. The test of finality, according to the court, is whether the order finally disposes of the rights of the parties, and if after the order, the order is made, the suit or proceeding still remains to be tried, after the order is rendered, the order will undoubtedly be a final order within the meaning of article 133(1) of the Constitution. [782 B E] (2) The expression 'final order ' in section 205(1) means an order finally determines the rights and obligations of the parties in dispute in a suit or proceeding from which appeal has arisen. [783 C] (3) The expression `final order ' is not a judgment or decree. The test is whether the final order disposes of the right of the parties and leave the rights of parties in dispute for determination in the suit or proceedings from which appeal is arisen. [883 D] (4) The test of final order is not a final order. The test has to be whether the order ultimately disposes of the interests of the parties. If the decision put an end to the suit, the order would undoubtedly be afinal order within the term of article 133 (1) of The Constitution. [882 E] (5) The test is not whether the order final disposes of the interest of the parties or not. If the order decides an important point or even a vital issue in the case, the order can undoubtedly be a preliminary order. [885 C] (6) The test has not been whether the order disposes of rights of the party or not. The test does not determine the rights and liabilities of the parties for determination in a suit. [886 D] (7) The test that is applied to an interlocutory order is whether the decision finally disposes of a right of the party and not whether the final decision disposes of the same or even a collateral issue in the suit. If the final decision is not a decree, the order may be deemed to be final. [887 E] (8) The test to be applied is whether the interim order is final and not a final decision. If the question is whether the ultimate decision disposes of a rights of the appellant, the order cannot be said to be final and the rights of other parties in relation to the matter in dispute in the suit are not final.

The appellant was appointed as a Head Clerk on June 1, 1963 by the Panchayat Samiti, Loharu, which was later on confirmed in that post. He was confirmed in that cadre on June 13, 1973. He was promoted as a Head clerk on June 1. 1963 by the Gram Panchayat. On January 21, 1974, he was confirmed in the post of Head Clerk. On January 1, 1974, the Panchayat Samiti lost its power to make appointments to the Panchayat Samiti. The appellant was appointed on June 1 1963 by the Loharu Panchayat Samiti in 1963. On January 31, 1974, a resolution was passed by the Gram Sabha that the appellant should be absorbed as a Head Clerks. The appellant, who was appointed as an Assistant Head Clerk on July 1, 1963, was confirmed in service in the Lohau Panchayat Samiti. On January 13, 1974, an order was passed by respondent 3 regularising the post of a Head Clerk. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court of Punjab and Haryana asking that he should be absorbed in Government service as a clerk in any event. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant was entitled to be absorbed in the Government service as an clerk in any case. The appellant contended that the Panchayat Samiti had lost its power under section 14(4) of the Amending Act to make appointments on a regular basis. The High court dismissed the writ application. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The right to be considered for promotion is a term and condition of service, which is required for the implementation of the schemes connected therewith and for such other duties and functions as may be assigned to them by the Panchayat Samitis. The appellant had, therefore, no right to be absorbed as an Assistant head Clerk. [775B] 2. The appellant 's appointment to the post of an Assistant Head clerk was lawfully to the post in which the Government has absorbed him. The appointment of the appellant to the post was lawfully to be recognised and protected, despite the fact that such appointment was made after June 13, 1974 when the Amending Act came into force. [776B] 3. The appellant could not, therefore, have appointed the appellant as a Head Peon on June 13. 1973. [778C] 4. The appellant having been appointed as a clerk prior to June 13,1973, the Panchayat Samitis lost its power in the post in question. The appellant cannot, therefore, be considered for appointment to the said post. [782D] 5. The appellant is, therefore, entitled to be considered in the post as a Head peon.

The appellants who were displaced persons from West Pakistan were granted quasipermanent allotment of 24 standard acres and 5 standard acres and 15 standard acres respectively. The Custodian General of Evacuee Property, Punjab, by a notification dated March 24, 1955, declared that the appellants were entitled to quasi permanent allotment of 24 Standard acres and 5 1/4 units of land. The appellants challenged the validity of the said notification by a writ petition under article 226 of the Constitution. The High Court held that the appellants had no right to a quasi permanent allotment and that the notification was invalid. The appellants contended that the Custodian General was not competent to revise the order under section 12(1) of the Act and the notification issued thereunder was invalid. Held, that the appellants could not be said to have been affected by the provisions of section 12(2) of the , and the notification under section 12 (1) of Act was not invalid. The Custodian was not competent under section 10 of the Act to revise the orders under section 12. The power of a managing officer or a managing corporation in the matter of cancellation of allotment was not affected by the provision of section 19(1) Of the Act. The power to cancel an allotment or to cancel an assignment was not affected either by the provisions Of section 19 or section 19 of the Act. Held, further, that the Custodian was not entitled to cancel an allotted or to cancel a lease made in favour of a person. The Custodian had no power to cancel the allotment in the absence of any provision in the Act or the notification. The Custodian could not cancel the allotment on the ground that the property vested in him. The Custodian, by reason of the divesting of the property, was empowered to manage evacuee property and in exercise of his power he will be competent to allot such property to any person or to cancel the lease or terminate a lease or terminate the lease or to cancel any allotment or lease made in his favour without the permission of a competent authority, or (c) has committed any act which is destructive of permanently or injurious to the property, or (d) has committed an act which is injurious to the interest or (e) has committed a act which is prejudicial to the interest of the Custodian. The Custodian is empowered to manage the evacuee property and to cancel an allotments or lease made under the Act.
