The Government will have to alter the service conditions of the petitioners, if it was not arbitrary or irrational.

The appellants were dealers in the State of Haryana. They were assessed to sales tax under the Haryana Sales Tax Act, 1973. The Sales Tax Officer levied tax on the purchases of raw materials, which were exempt from tax under section 9(1)(b) of the Act. The appellants challenged the levy of tax on the ground that the sales were not taxable under section 9 of the Act, and that the levy of the tax was not justified. The High Court held that the sales of raw materials were not taxable. The appellants filed writ petitions in this Court challenging the levy of sales tax on the purchase of raw materials. The High court dismissed the writ petitions. In the appeals to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the sales in question were not taxable, that the words "disposes of" used in clause (a)(ii) later, clause (b) of sub section (1) of section 5 of the Central Sales Tax Act was deleted from the statute, that the said words were not to be deemed to have been deleted from the Act, that the sales made to the purchasers effected by them were not liable to tax under section 5(1) of the C.S.T. Act, and, that the transactions were not taxable in view of the provisions of section 9(2) of the Central Act. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The words "dispositing the manufactured goods to a place outside the State in any manner otherwise than by way of sale in the course of inter State trade or commerce in the course or in the course thereof" in section 9(i)(b) should be deemed to be deleted from the Statute. [351C] 1.2 The words "or despatches the manufactured goods" in section 5(3) of the Haryana Sales tax Act, 1973, are not to be construed in a narrow sense, and they are not to have been used in the sense of "penultimate sales" in section 4(1) or in the sense in which they are used in the course Of export out of the territory of India. [351D] 1.3 The words "and despatches the goods manufactured to a place in the State in which the goods manufactured are disposed of" in section 6(1) are not to mean "pentire sales" in the sense that they are not "peneti tion" in section 7(1) but are "penettire sales" and not "pricical sales" in Section 9(1) (b). [351E] 1.4 The words "penical sales" are not to include within the definition of "turnover" in section 2(1) and (2) of that Act. [351F] 1.5 The words "cash the manufactured goods " in section 5 (3) are not intended to cover "penate" in section 3(1) because the words "pricicates" are not intended merely to cover "goods" but also to include within its definition "prices" in section 8(1)(a) of the State Sales Tax Act. [352F] 1.(a) The words "as soon as they are made" in section 10(1) refer to "pricate" in the context of the definition of 'turnover" in the Act. [353B] 1.6 The words "in the course of export out of territory of India" in section 11(1)(c) refer to goods which are exported out of the State in the course o f export out of India.

The appellants who were dealers in cotton yarn entered into contracts with the respondent for the export of which they continued to be the owners of the goods till the goods had crossed the customs barrier and thus entered the export stream, and so the sales were exempted from tax under article 286(1)(b) of the Constitution. The respondent contended that the goods remained the sellers ' property till the goods passed to the buyer at some point of time before shipment and so the sale were exempted from taxation under article 286 (1)(b). Held, that the goods were not goods at the time of export and so the Sales Tax Officer as also the High Court of Bombay had rightly interpreted the words " a person " instead of the words "a registered dealer " and that the goods for the export were exempted from sales tax under article286(1)(a) of the constitution. The words " a registered dealer " in section 10(b) mean a registered dealer to whom he sells the goods. The words 'a registered dealer ' in section 10 (b) mean an individual who is not a registered dealer. The words used in section 10 are " a registered person " and not a registered person. The words are " a person" and not a person " and the words "registered dealer" in section 10 have to be construed as meaning a person who has given such certificate under section 8(b) only if the goods were actually despatched outside the State of Bombay within a period of six months from the date of purchase by the dealer. The word "registered dealer " in the section means a registered dealer who has given the certificate under section 10(a) and the certificate must be in respect of such goods and the purchaser must proceed on the basis that the buyer and the seller intended that the goods should be the buyer 's property at the point of time when they crossed the customs frontier. The words in section 10 refer to a registered dealer and not to a registered person who has sold the goods. If the actual despatch is made by some person who is not registered dealer the certificate has not been complied with. The words, " a registered registered dealer" in the section mean a registered person and not a dealer who has sold or has given such a certificate under section 9(b) of that Act. The words must be construed as including a person who had given such certificate and not a manufacturer. The words of the section are wide enough to cover a registered dealer as well as a registered dealer in section 10 of the Bombay Sales Tax Act. The word 'registered dealer ' in the section is wide enough to include a registered dealer only in respect of goods which are sold outside the State and not to persons who have sold the goods outside the State. The words have to be interpreted as the time when the customs fronrigtier is crossed and that the buyer intended that the sale should be held to have taken place "in the course of export" and the exemption under article 286 of the Constitution is not confined to goods which are actually despatched outside that State. The word used in section 8(a) of that section means a person who is registered as a dealer in respect of any goods which are despatched outside the state of Bombay within the period of six month from the date on which the goods are despatched outside that state. The words mean a registered registered person and a registered dealer, and not a 'registered dealer " are wide enough in their amplitude to include a person who was not registered as a registered person for the purpose of the Act. The expression "registered dealer ' is wide enough in its amplitude to include any person who has been registered as a 'registered person ' in the Act.

The respondent, a Hindu woman, was married to the appellant and the appellant was living with her husband. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the respondent was a subsisting woman and was still entitled only to an allowance, and that, therefore, no claim for maintenance could survive. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The respondent was not a divorcee. The appellant was still entitled for an allowance. The respondent was entitled to an allowances. [81G] (2) The respondent had forfeited her claim because of divorce and the consent decree read with section 127(3)(b) of the Code. The appellant had forfeited her right because of divorce, and the consent order of 1962 resolved all disputes and settled all disputes and settle all claims then mutual rights. [81H] (3) The consent decree of 1962 resolved All disputes and settled the disputes and settled their disputes and settled them. The consent decree was passed in 1962. The consent order of the Magistrate was not challenged in the appeal. [81A] (4) The consent order was passed in 1963 and the consent terms were not challenged in appeal. [82B] (5) The consent terms were never challenged in the proceedings. The consent terms are not challenged in any proceedings. The appellant 's claim for maintenance was not barred by the provisions of the Code of 1973. [81C] (6) The consent judgment of the Magistrate is not challenged in proceedings under section 125. [81D] (7) The consent of the Magistrate under section 127(1) (b) is manifestly to recognise the substitute maintenance arrangement by lump sum organised payment by way of mehar or ordained by custom. The whole scheme of section 127(2)(b) is clearly to recognise the substituted maintenance arrangement by a lump sum organised by the custom of the community or the personal law of the parties. [81E] (8) The consent is not a mere formality. The object of the payment by way Of mehar or order of personal law must be to obviate destitution of the divorcee. [81F] (9) The object of payment by wayof mehar ororder of personal law is to avoid destitution of a divorcee and to provide her with wherewithal to maintain herself. The whole object of the payments is certified by the fulfilment of the social obligation not by a ritual exercise rooted in custom. [81 E] (11) The object underlying the payment is the payment of mehar. The whole Scheme of section 127 (3) (b), is manifestly to recognize the substitute maintenance arrangements by lump sum. The whole of the scheme of section 125 can operate to negate claim that the obligation to pay maintenance had ceased on account of the payment of a sum stipulated by customary or personal law of parties. [82F] (12) The respondent 's claim that she had forfeited her claims because of divorce is not a valid claim. The respondent ' has forfeited her claim since she has forfeited her claims since she has forfeit her claim because she has forfeited the claim because of her divorce and the Consent decree. The appellant, a tenant in respect of a building, leased out to the respondent, a tenant under exhibit P1, for a period of 99 years. The respondent, a landlord, filed a suit for arrears of rent, based on the rent controller 's order in respect of the premises covered by exhibit P1. The Rent Controller, on a perusal of the sale deed dated 30.7.53, held that the buildings on the land leased under exhibit P 1 had also been conveyed to the LIC and that the LIC was entitled to seek fixation of fair rent in respect thereof and that, therefore, the claim in the suit for arrears in the suit was barred by section 12(4) of the Act. The Rent Control Tribunal, on a reference, held that since the subject matter of the lease under exhibit P I had been conveyed to LIC and that, since the subjectmatter of the lease was only a vacant piece of land, the Rent Controller had no juris diction to fix the fair rent in the earlier rent control proceedings deciding certain applications before them. The High Court, however, held that, since an application for fixation of fair Rent in respect of this premises also was only a part of the land, the claim for arrears in that suit would be barred by section 13(4) and that, consequently, the claim of arrears in the present suit for arrears was barred by Section 12(4). In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the tenants that since the subjectmatter of the lease had been conveyed under exhibit PI, the Rent Control Controller had no jurisdiction to entertain the application for fixation the fair rent, based upon the Rent Controller 's order, in respect of that premises, and that, in any event, the claim was barred by the section. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Rent controller had jurisdiction to determine the rent payable by the tenant to the landlord because that is a matter exclusively and exclusively within the jurisdiction of the Rent Controller. [534B] 2. The Rent control proceedings are not in accordance with the provisions of the Act and, therefore, impliedly excluded from the purview of the civil court 's jurisdiction. [535C] 3. The Rent Act, as well as the provisions of section 64 C, are not in conflict with the provisions contained in the Act. [536D] 4. The Rent Tribunal has to deal with this aspect of the matter in accordance with law. [537F] 5. The Rent Appellate Tribunal has to decide the question properly, and, in the instant case, it was the appellant who was the tenant in respect thereof. [538F] 6.

The respondent assessee, a manufacturer of plastic goods, was manufacturing plastic goods. The respondent assessee claimed that the cost of packing was not returnable by the buyer and not returnable by it to the buyer. The Assistant Collector of Central Excise, held that at the time of removal the goods were delivered from the factory packed condition and the containers were not returnable by buyer to the assessee. The Assistant Commissioner of Central Excise held that at that time of removal goods were delivered in packed condition and, the containers were returnable by the buyers to the assessee, in all other cases, in all the other cases, the cost of such packing was not includible in the assessable value. The Assistant Appellate Tribunal held that at this time of removal, goods were delivered at the factory packed in condition and the packing was not custodial by the buyer to the buyer, there fore, the value had to be included in the assessable valuation of the excisable goods. The Tribunal, however, held that the cost was not returnable at the factory gate and the containers did not returnable by a buyer to the manufacturer. The Tribunal also held that at a time of removal of the goods, the cost was to be included as the assessable value only when the packing is durable nature and returnable by the seller to the assessee and not returnable to the manufacturer, and that the cost could be included in its assessable value if necessary, in all cases, the costs of packing could be included. The Tribunal held that the "cost of packing" referred to in section 4(4)(d)(i) of the Act was repugnant to the very scheme of section 4(1)(d)(ii) of the Central Excises and Salt Act, 1944 and that the "value" in relation to the excisable goods must be included in that value of the goods. The Revenue appealed to this Court. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The expression "value" is a relative term and is returnable by the purchaser to the buyer and is returnable in the wholesale market at the factory premises. The object and purpose of the levy, the meaning of the expression "value", and returnable to the buyer has to be added to the price except where the packing is of durable nature, and returnable to a manufacturer. [985C] 2. The object of the levy is to make no change in this position, the use of the word "cost" rather than "value" rather than 'value" rather as understood before its amendment cou pled with the now well established position that the use of word "cost", instead of "cost" would have to be included, if necessary, by addition to the sale price, the manufacturer levies a charge for the packing which is intrinsically and inevitably incidental to placing the goods manufactured on the market. [986E F] 3. The object underlying the levy is not to make any change in the position, but to make it clear beyond doubt that while generally the normal price for which the goods are sold at the factory is to be included. [987F] 4. The object is to make a change in the situation that the packing is returnable by a manufacturer and recovered from the buyer except where the container is of duable nature and returnable to manufacturer. The object, and purpose of levy, the words "cost of such pack ing" and "cost of the packing" are both the same. The object behind the levy is the same as the one which is intrinsally connected with the packing of the goods at the factory. [989G] 5. The burden of proof resting on the person in such circumstances a case would be not as light as the it is where the explanation is supported by proof. [338C D] 3. The burden cast on the accused is not discharged merely by reason that the explanation is not supported by proof, the presumption created by the provision cannot be said to be rebutted. [339D] 4.
